results.title: AI Inference: Key Innovations for 2025 - AI News and Updates - AI Business & Insights Hub
results.content: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving, particularly in the realm of inference, which bridges model training and real-world applications. This article delves into the current landscape of AI inference, highlighting its significance and optimization strategies. Inference is critical for making real-time predictions based on trained models. Innovations like quantization, pruning, and specialized hardware are essential for optimizing inference performance. Chrunner raises crucial points about hardware and model compression, but I’m seeing a shift toward *design-time optimization* as the next frontier. In medical imaging AI, this approach cut inference latency by 40% on edge devices without sacrificing diagnostic precision. Beyond hardware and model compression, I’m intrigued by how inference location strategies will evolve. Building on the orchestration challenges Tolisoul raised, I’m struck by how little attention goes to *inference-time data pipelines* as a bottleneck. Take autonomous vehicles: real-time LiDAR point cloud processing often consumes over 30% of total inference latency. Building on the infrastructure discussion, I’m tracking a crucial software-layer shift: **adaptive inference engines** that dynamically reconfigure compilation based on real-time hardware states. NVIDIA’s upcoming runtime for autonomous vehicles exemplifies this—if GPU temperatures spike during dense object detection, it instantly switches to sparser neural network branches without crashing latency SLAs. This moves beyond pre-defined edge/cloud splits by letting *local hardware conditions* dictate optimization strategies. For instance, autonomous vehicles using ultra-optimized models for split-second decisions could sacrifice interpretability layers critical for accident analysis. As we shrink models and distribute inference, are we inadvertently making AI *less accountable*? We’re seeing early warnings in healthcare: AI-assisted surgery systems now use real-time adaptive models to optimize instrument tracking, but when a anomalous movement occurs, the “why” gets buried under layers of optimization. What if we treated explainability like a real-time SLA—not as overhead, but as a core optimization constraint? Adaptive inference introduces a new layer of opacity: not just from model compression, but from the runtime’s own decision logic. Beyond just stripping explainability layers, I’m seeing optimization create *new forms of opacity*—like federated learning systems where models trained across thousands of devices hide problematic data patterns in aggregated updates. Consider autonomous vehicles—current systems optimize for inference speed, but if a car swerves unexpectedly, the “why” is often lost in quantized layers.

results.title: Latency, the Ultimate Gen AI Constraint
results.content: To make sense of the latency constraint, we need to analyze what happens under the hood when an AI autocomplete suggestion is made:. However, these transformer models are also what are termed “autoregressive,” which essentially means that the latency scales linearly with (the length of the input text + the length of the output text). However this means that you add extra latency around the inference. You can send the request over the network to the API, but if they are doing any sort of rate limiting or scheduling logic (likely), you may add even more latency before you get a response. If you have high concurrency and want to have no additional latency between request coming in and performing an inference, then you will need a lot of hardware and that is expensive. Using the Characters per Opportunity metric, we can actually point to the effect of latency on the value of an AI autocomplete tool. Feedback rate is primarily affected by latency (the suggestion isn’t produced in time before the developer has made the next keystroke) and suggestion confidence (the suggestion is produced in time, but the tool deems it not useful enough to show to a developer). For example, if you are producing longer suggestions, then the latency may drop the feedback rate, but perhaps the increase in average tokens per acceptance makes up for it. That being said, arithmetic operations in fp16 are much more expensive latency-wise than if they were stored in int8 or int4 (8 and 4 bits respectively) and given that GPUs have a max amount of memory, using 16 bits per weight puts a cap on the size of a model that you can even serve on a single GPU because swapping in weights of a model in-and-out GPU memory during inference is a very large latency hit. * Model parallelism: As mentioned under quantization, a GPU has a max amount of memory, so even with every other trick, there is still an upper limit on the size of a model that can be served on a single GPU since latency forces storing all of the weights in memory simultaneously. This ends up giving a similar stellar latency with even larger models, which means higher quality suggestions.

results.title: Efficient Deep Learning for ADAS/AV Through Systematic Pruning and Quantization
results.content: Berkeley DeepDrive | We seek to merge deep learning with automotive perception and bring computer vision technology to the forefront. Efficient Deep Learning for ADAS/AV Through Systematic Pruning and Quantization #### At a glance An important barrier in the deployment of deep neural networks is latency, which is critical for autonomous driving tasks. High latency can lead to delayed recognition of an object or a pedestrian in front of the car, making it challenging to take the appropriate maneuver in time. For this reason, practitioners have been forced to use shallow networks with non-ideal accuracy to avoid this latency problem. We plan to address this challenge by developing a systematic multi-faceted approach for end-to-end efficient NN design and deployment by pursuing the following thrusts: (i) developing a fast coupled quantization and pruning framework that allows the practitioner to obtain optimal trade-offs between accuracy, and speed for a given latency constraint; (ii) developing a quantization and pruning aware Neural Architecture Search co-designed for a target hardware platform for autonomous driving with limited power budget; and (iii) focusing on object detection and segmentation applications with 4K video stream. The outcome of this work will be an open-source framework that will automatically find an efficient NN architecture for the application-specific constraints of accuracy, latency, model size, and power consumption. This will build upon our recent works on quantization~\cite{dong2019hawq,dong2019hawqv2,yao2020hawqv3,cai2020zeroq}, pruning~\cite{yu2021hessian}, NAS~\cite{wu2018mixed,wu2019fbnet}, and the corresponding open source codes that have been contributed to BDD repository~\cite{hawqcode,zeroqcode,hapcode,pyhessian,fbnetcode}. This is a continuation of the completed project: "Efficient Neural Networks Through Systematic Quantization" and the work in these projects have laid the groundwork for "Real-time and Accurate Object Detection through Systematic Quantization of Transformer and MLP-based Computer Vision Models". #### Address ©2025 The Regents of the University of California.
